subtype: Approach: building a minimum viable version in six weeks [Action]
passage: Six weeks. That's what we gave ourselves. Himani and I sat in a borrowed room in Lucknow and built the ugliest invoicing tool you have ever seen, out of no-code tools and a spreadsheet. No custom backend, no login screen, nothing you would show in a pitch. I'm Gopika, by the way. At the end of week six we walked into twenty kirana shops with a phone, sat next to the shop owners and asked them to try it. Three said it was useless. Seven said they would pay if it printed in Hindi. One old shopkeeper pointed out that a button I would never have noticed was the wrong colour. We would have spent a year on the backend if we hadn't asked. Instead we spent our time fixing what people actually said.

qa.q: How many shop owners did Gopika and Himani show the tool to?
qa.a: They showed it to twenty shop owners.

qa.q: What does "the ugliest invoicing tool you have ever seen" suggest about how Gopika felt about showing it?
qa.a: It suggests Gopika felt a little embarrassed but was willing to show unfinished work anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could have worked instead of building a backend first?
qa.a: They could have asked shop owners about their invoicing habits first, or run the process by hand, because that also gets feedback before large work.

qa.q: How might the shop owners have felt being asked to try it?
qa.a: They may have felt listened to, since their comments about Hindi printing and the button colour were used.

grounding: Two founders build a bare-bones invoicing tool in six weeks with no-code tools and put it in front of twenty shop owners in Lucknow first.

subtype: Approach: building a minimum viable version in six weeks [Action]
passage:
Two young men came into my shop in Aminabad one afternoon while I was weighing dal. Nilesh and Tejas, they said, with a tablet. They wanted to show me a billing tool. Nothing fancy: a form, a list of my usual items, a button that printed a bill on a small printer they had brought. Tejas said they had put it together in six weeks without writing any real code, and that mine was the eleventh of twenty shops they were visiting.
I tried it for a sale of rice and soap. The item list had no ghee, and the bill had no space for customers who buy on credit. Nilesh wrote both things in his notebook. Tejas asked, "Would you pay for this if it had those?" I said maybe.
They came back ten days later. The ghee was there. So was a credit column.

qa.q: What two things did Nilesh write in his notebook?
qa.a: The item list had no ghee, and the bill had no space for customers who buy on credit.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he asked "Would you pay for this?"
qa.a: He was probably hopeful and a little anxious to learn whether the bare tool had real value to shopkeepers.

qa.q: What did the founders' approach get right?
qa.a: They put a simple six-week version in front of real shop owners before building more, and fixed what users actually needed.

qa.q: How does the shopkeeper see the tool after ten days?
qa.a: The shopkeeper sees that they listened, since ghee and a credit column were added, which may turn that maybe into a yes.

grounding: It shows two founders taking a bare-bones billing tool built without custom code to twenty Lucknow shops before building anything bigger.

subtype: Approach: building a minimum viable version in six weeks [Action]
passage:
Week 1, Monday. In a borrowed room in Gomti Nagar, Keerthana and Anand stick a sheet on the wall: "Six weeks. Twenty kirana shops. No custom code." Anand, who wants to build a proper backend, groans. Keerthana says, "Not until twenty shopkeepers tell us what's wrong with it."
Week 4, Thursday. Their bare billing tool, made with drag-and-drop form builders and a spreadsheet, crashes when Mr Qureshi adds his fortieth item. Anand patches it at midnight. Keerthana visits three more shops and writes down every complaint: too many taps, Hindi item names missing.
Week 6, Saturday. Twenty shops have tried it. Nine use it daily; four say they would pay. Anand finally opens his code editor. Now, he says, he knows exactly what to build.

qa.q: How many shops said they would pay?
How did Anand feel about the no-custom-code rule at first?
qa.a: He was frustrated and impatient, groaning because he wanted to build a proper backend.

qa.q: What did testing with twenty shops give them that building first would not?
qa.a: Real complaints like too many taps and missing Hindi item names, so the proper backend can be built around what shopkeepers need.

qa.q: What is it like for Mr Qureshi to use such an early version?
qa.a: Mr Qureshi hits a crash at his fortieth item, which is annoying, but it gets fixed quickly and his problem shapes the product.

grounding: It shows two founders shipping a bare-bones billing tool in six weeks with no custom code and putting it in front of twenty Lucknow shopkeepers first.
